Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Redirection: I think of something else, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Megan, a 41-year-old firefighter with fourteen years on the job, had always taken pride in her physical resilience. Then came the meningitis. What began as a blinding headache and stiff neck spiraled into septic shock, a ten‑day ICU stay, and a series of lumbar punctures and central lines that she could never bring herself to describe aloud. When she tried, the words dissolved into a surge of heat, a tightness in her chest, and an involuntary stillness—her body locking into the same prone, helpless position she had occupied on that hospital bed, watching the fluorescent lights flicker above while a nurse adjusted the IV drip. The terror that washed over her then, raw and wordless, returned intact each time a memory surfaced, as if no time had passed at all.

Returning to work six months later, Megan found that the station itself had become a minefield. The bleach-based cleaner used to disinfect the bunker gear carried a faint, hospital-like odor that made her stomach clench and her palms sweat whenever she walked past the decontamination bay. She began to scan her environment constantly—for the sharp gleam of a needle, for the sight of an ambulance pulling into the bay, for any sound that might signal a medical call. Her body stayed wired, muscles braced, ready to react, even during quiet nights at the station. Every routine health log reading or minor cough among her crew sharpened her vigilance; she was certain, on some level, that any sign of physical compromise could herald another collapse.

She started to avoid emotional intensity entirely. When a fellow firefighter shared a difficult story from a call, Megan would nod and excuse herself, finding a task in the apparatus bay. At home with her husband, she deflected conversations about her recovery—redirecting her mind to the next meal, the schedule for the week, anything to block the images before they fully formed. She also avoided medical cues with a discipline that had begun to erode her professional standing. On medical emergency dispatches, she would offer to swap with a colleague for a fire run, or she’d linger in the engine bay until the ambulance left without her. Twice she was reprimanded for not taking her turn on paramedic training; she explained it away as “bad timing,” but her captain noticed the pattern. The avoidance extended to her own health: she skipped routine physicals and ignored a lingering fatigue, rationalizing that the hospital waiting room would trigger a panic she could not afford.

The most difficult consequence was the growing distance from her husband. He had been her constant support during the illness, but now Megan pulled away from any conversation that risked strong emotion. She preferred quiet evenings with the television on, her mind trained to drift elsewhere. He tried to ask about how she was feeling; she gave short answers and moved to another room. She knew he was hurt, but the alternative—letting herself feel the fear that hummed beneath her skin—felt far more dangerous.

What finally brought Megan to the department’s employee assistance program was a routine training drill. A mannequin was set up with an IV line and a simulated wound. The moment Megan saw the tubing, the antiseptic smell of the training room hit her, and her body snapped into that same hospital‑bed stillness. She could not move or speak; she only felt her heart hammering against her ribs, the old terror flooding back. The training officer had to guide her outside. Her captain told her gently that she needed to talk to someone.

Now Megan sits in the clinician’s office, unable to put her experience into words. She is afraid that the simple act of speaking will break something open inside her, yet she is equally afraid of continuing to live this way—always braced, always scanning, always pulling away from the people she loves most. She wants to feel safe again, even if she is not sure what safety looks like anymore.
